issue.title: The EU deal: food, carbon and young people, and who pays for student fees
issue.question: How much should Britain give up to get closer trade and travel with the EU, and who should pay if EU students get home fees?
issue.summary: At the UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November 2026 the two sides agreed a food and farm trade deal, a link between their carbon markets and a youth scheme for 18 to 31 year olds. The government says the package could add up to 0.5% to UK GDP by 2040, about £17 billion a year. The youth scheme is capped and visa-based, with no access to benefits. Both sides also agreed to work towards a deal on tuition fees within six months; EU officials want EU students to pay UK home rates, and the UK disputes that this is linked to the rest of the deal.
issue.slot_reason: EU trade had not come up yet in the simulation, and the UK-EU summit deal was in the UK news that day.

news.headline: UK and EU agree food trade, carbon market link and youth scheme at Brussels summit

poll.finding: 68% supported (32% strongly, 36% somewhat) and 16% opposed negotiating a deal that would let up to 200,000 18-30 year olds from the UK study and work in the EU for up to four years, with the same for EU young people in the UK; 16% did not know. This is the most recent poll on a youth scheme question that I could open, it is two years older than the news and a different version of the scheme from the one agreed (three years, 100,000 each way), so no single share is set.

bench.title: Home fees for EU students, but capped, reciprocal and costed in public
bench.answer: Keep the current fee system and universities; change the terms of the tuition deal due within six months (s4). Home-rate fees would apply to EU students only inside a fixed yearly cap on places, set by ministers and kept separate from places for UK students, so none are cut. The deal would start only when the EU gives UK students equal fees. The Treasury would publish the yearly gap and fund it from a named budget line, not from NHS or school money. Parliament would review it after three years, and the cap shrinks or the deal ends if the gap passes the published limit. It worked if UK places hold, the gap stays inside the limit, and UK students use the reciprocal rate. The Russell Group warns that any cut to EU student fees would put pressure on UK places (s4).

bench.title: A joint fees board, not a trade-off behind closed doors
bench.answer: Take the fee question out of the wider trade talks and give it to a joint UK-EU fees board with equal seats for UK students, EU students and universities, plus a fixed budget. The two governments would set that up within weeks, inside the six months they have already agreed for a fees deal (s4). Times Higher Education reports EU officials saying the rest of the deal hangs on fees, and the UK side disputing that (s4), so a separate board lets the food, carbon and youth parts go ahead. The Russell Group warns that any fee cut would put pressure on UK places (s4), and 26 simulated citizens set a limit of no free places paid by taxpayers, so the board's pot must be named and capped. It worked if the rest of the deal is not held up, the fee rate is published, and UK places do not fall.

bench.title: Trade access, but let students steer the fee bargain
bench.answer: In this simulation, Britain should accept shared food and carbon rules for easier trade, but offer home fees only with equal terms for UK students abroad. Fee talks are still open (s4). Parliament should set that bargain. Elected student and staff boards at each university should check its costs. Employers wanting to recruit through the youth scheme should fund any fee gap through a charge for taking part. No signed funding, no fee concession. Publish the accounts each year. Judge success by cheaper food, shorter border waits, students travelling both ways, falling emissions and no lost university places or courses.

gate.verdict: No answer passes every test. A fails the limit on taxpayers paying; C passes it; most of the rest cannot be settled by facts. Who should pay for fees is a values question.

jury.question: If EU students get home fees, who should pay the gap between home and international fees?
options: Taxpayers, from a named, capped budget line that is published each year
Employers who recruit through the youth scheme, by a charge
No one here: home fees only for countries that give UK students the same rate back
No home fees: say no and keep the rest of the deal, even if the EU objects
jury.ruling: No one here: home fees only for countries that give UK students the same rate back. Four of twelve jurors chose it, the most of any option, because they wanted fair terms both ways and no new bill.

reasons.text: Reciprocal terms are the honest deal. Nobody here should pay more.
Closer ties matter. Pay for it openly from a named line, with a cap, and publish it.
Employers get the workers. Let them pay a charge, not us.
I won't pay fees for others while my own family struggles. Keep the rest of the deal.

minister.trial: In the six-month fee talks, the UK offers home-rate fees only to students from EU countries that give UK students the same rate back, in writing. Start with up to two such countries for one intake year. No new cost to UK taxpayers. Parliament sees the terms.
minister.fail_number: Any extra taxpayer cost for the trial (target: 0p), or fewer than 1 EU country signing equal terms by the stop date.
minister.statement: The jury was split, and I will say so. Four of twelve wanted fees only when the other side gives the same back. Three wanted taxpayers to pay openly. Three said no to home fees at all. Two wanted employers to pay. So I'm signing one small thing. Home rates only for countries that match them, one intake year, nothing added to anyone's tax bill. EU officials say the rest of the deal hangs on fees, Times Higher Education reports. The UK side says the parts are separate. Either way, this offer stands on its own. If no country signs equal terms by the autumn, it failed, and I'll say so.
